1:
Henry fixes on how poor the triumph looked. He rode an ass’s colt, contemptible for being an ass and, being a colt, rough and untrimmed; and it was borrowed, as much else had been — Christ went upon the water in a borrowed boat, ate the passover in a borrowed chamber, was buried in a borrowed sepulchre, and here rode on a borrowed colt. Yet he came publicly: he did not steal into the city incognito, as one that durst not show his face, and his disciples might see how bravely their Master defied his enemies. Pseudo-Chrysostom denies any necessity in the ride, since he had gone over Judaea and Galilee on foot, and calls the action typical. Bede reads the contrast doctrinally: in John he fled lest they make him king, but now, coming to Jerusalem to suffer, he does not shun those who call him king, that he might openly teach he was King over an empire not earthly but everlasting in the heavens, the path to it lying through contempt of death.

The colt draws four notes. Clarke says why it mattered that none had sat on it: no animal put to domestic use was allowed in sacred uses even among the heathen, and those never yoked were held sacred — he quotes the Delphic oracle in Ovid, bidding a man seek a lonely cow, unworn with yokes, unbroken to the plough. Ellicott notes that Mark, with Luke and John, omits the she-ass on which Matthew lays stress as fulfilling the prophecy; whereon never man sat is in Mark and Luke only. Theophylact wonders at the owners letting it go: they would not have allowed it, had not the Divine power been upon them, being country folk and farmers. Augustine settles the discrepancy: where both may be the case there is no disagreement, though one Evangelist mentions one thing and another a second. Ambrose turns the tethering into allegory: it was bound before the door, because whosoever is not in Christ is without, in the way, where no man has certain possession, and miserable is his service whose rights are unfixed, for he who has not the one Master has many. Strangers bind him to possess him; Christ looses him to keep him, knowing that gifts are stronger ties than bonds.

Hosanna is disputed. Bede takes it for a Hebrew word made of two — hosy, save, and anna, a supplicatory interjection, as the Latin heu is an exclamation of grief. Theophylact reports that some make it save me and others a hymn, and thinks the former more probable. Pseudo-Jerome reads it save us, that men might be saved by him who came in the name of the Lord; Pseudo-Chrysostom takes Hosanna in the highest as praise to the God of all. Pseudo-Jerome also gives a reason for the pairing of the messengers: they are called two by two and sent two by two, since charity implies more than one, for woe to him that is alone.

On the shout Ellicott observes that blessing the kingdom as well as the king is another touch distinguishing Mark’s record. Gill explains the title: the Jews more usually called Abraham their father, but because the Messiah was David’s son they call David so here. Clarke notes that in the name of the Lord is omitted by several manuscripts and dropped by one editor. Cyril of Jerusalem takes that phrase back to Exodus, where the Lord proclaims the name of the Lord before Moses — being himself the Lord, what Lord does he proclaim? — and finds the Father and the Son covertly taught. Robertson notes that Bethphage and Bethany stand together here as in Luke, though Matthew names only Bethphage; Wesley, that the limits of Bethany reached the mount of Olives and joined Bethphage, so our Lord was come where the two met. Barnes adds that the entry was public.
11:
He goes first to the temple, and looks. Bede draws a rule from it: entering the temple first shows us a form of religion, that wherever we find a house of prayer we should turn aside to it first. He notes the poverty too: in so large a city Christ found no host, but lodged in a country place, teaching in the temple by day and going out at night. Barnes explains that the temple here means the courts, not the edifice, Christ not being of the tribe of Levi; he saw there the abominations he afterwards corrected. Lightfoot gets more from the looking: the word means not a bare beholding but a beholding with reproof, which among the Jews was admonition. Ellicott defends the account, the minuteness of Mark’s report being evidence in its favour, and allows eventide covered the hours before sunset. Theophylact reads the going in and out mystically, to show he left the temple desolate and open to the spoiler; Pseudo-Jerome compresses the day into a sentence — he went in the morning to the Jews, and visits us in the eventide of the world.

Calvin takes up the difficulty this raises. Mark appears to differ from Matthew and Luke, who have the traders driven out at once, where he says only that Christ looked round, throwing the cleansing to the next day. Calvin answers that Mark, not having spoken of the purifying at the time, inserts it afterwards out of its proper place, so the stricter order makes no contradiction.

Why he came to the tree is disputed. Henry keeps it plain: he went from Bethany without breakfast and was hungry, being subject to all the sinless infirmities of our nature. Chrysostom will not have it: how was he hungry in the morning, if not that by an economy he permitted it to his flesh, and what prevented him eating before he left Bethany? He came principally to curse the tree, for his disciples’ sake, that they might have faith; he everywhere blessed and punished none, yet it was right to prove his chastising power, and, unwilling to prove it on men, he showed it on a plant. Theophylact says the same: he showed he could in a moment exterminate those about to crucify him.

The clause about the season divides them. Clarke argues it means the season of gathering was not yet, marshalling parallels where the word bears that sense. Lightfoot answers from horticulture: there was a fig called Benoth Shuach which never wanted leaves nor figs, bearing yearly though the fruit did not ripen till the third year; such he supposes this tree. Ellicott sees no need for either device: the precocious foliage suggested early figs, but the tree was no exception to its kind. Robertson puts it in three words — promise without performance. Wesley settles it by the design of the parable, to reprove the Jewish Church for unfruitfulness at the season when fruit might best be expected; Gill notes only that the tree stood at a distance.

On the curse Robertson observes that the verb is an optative, a wish which negated makes a curse, and that the disciples listened in amazement, it being no fault of the tree that it had put out leaves. Cyril of Jerusalem supplies the typology none of the others reach. Adam received the sentence that the ground was cursed and should bring forth thorns; for this cause Jesus assumes the thorns, to cancel the sentence, and was buried in the earth, that the cursed earth might receive blessing. At the time of the sin they clothed themselves with fig leaves, and for this cause Jesus made the fig tree the last of his signs, cursing that one alone for the figure’s sake. Was he ignorant that a tree bears no fruit out of season? No, but knowing it he came as if seeking.
15:
Bede ties the two acts together: what the Lord had done in figure when he cursed the barren fig tree he now shows openly by casting the wicked out of the temple, the fig tree being not in fault, in having no fruit before its time, but the priests blameable. He allows what was sold was probably necessary for the ministry of the place, and argues from the lesser: if the Lord forbids in the temple worldly matters men might freely do elsewhere, how much more do they deserve heaven’s anger who carry on there what is unlawful anywhere. Then he turns the doves into a doctrine: because the Holy Spirit appeared over the Lord in the shape of a dove, the gifts of the Spirit are fitly pointed out under that name, and the Dove is sold when the laying on of hands is sold for a price. Theophylact carries the figure the other way: if a man by sinning gives up to the devil the grace of his baptism, he has sold his Dove, and is cast out of the temple. He also explains the name of thieves, who always troop together for gain, and observes that it turns to the greater condemnation of the Jews, who though the Lord did this so often did not correct their conduct.

Augustine raises the question of order, and answers it his own way. John relates it very differently, wherefore it is manifest that not once only but twice this was done by the Lord, the first time related by John and the last by the other three. Mark again does not keep Matthew’s order; and since Matthew has him go out to Bethany and return in the morning to curse the tree, Matthew more probably kept the order of time, Mark passing over what was done the first day and inserting it later.

The vessel prohibition is peculiar to Mark. Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic rule behind it: none was to go into the Mountain of the Temple with staff, shoes, purse, or dust upon his feet, nor make it a common thoroughfare, the same being ordered of a synagogue, even one laid waste; and he cites the rabbi who, asked how he had lived so long, answered that he had never made a synagogue a thoroughfare. Robertson says the authorities had prohibited the outer court as a short cut to the mount of Olives, but the rule was neglected and irreverent conduct went on there. Ellicott agrees men were using the courts as a short cut, and takes the vessels for baskets and implements of traffic; Clarke notes the Jewish word had a vast latitude, covering arms, clothes and instruments of music. Wesley draws the inference: so strong notions had our Lord of even relative holiness, and of the regard due to places, as well as times, dedicated to God.

Pseudo-Jerome identifies the two halves, the house of prayer from Isaiah and the den of thieves from Jeremiah. Robertson notes that for all the nations is in Mark alone, and will not soften what follows: Jesus assumes and exercises Messianic authority and dares to smite this political and financial abuse; some deny a preacher the right to denounce such abuses in business and politics even when they invade morals and religion, but Jesus did not hesitate. On the effect, the Gloss cites Amos, that they hate him who rebuketh in the gate, and observes that from this wicked design they were kept back a time solely by fear. Barnes reads that fear as envy: he became popular, the Pharisees saw their authority destroyed, and sought his life. Ellicott notes that they feared him is again peculiar to Mark, who omits the healing of the blind and lame and the children crying Hosanna; Gill adds that one copy reads that they came again, having been there the day before.
19:
When the tree withered comes first. Theophylact grants that Matthew has it dried at once, while Mark has them see it on the morrow, and finds no perplexity: Matthew means they saw it not at once but the next day. Augustine puts it more sharply: it dried not when they saw it but immediately after the word of the Lord, for they saw it not beginning to wither but wholly withered. Robertson notes that Matthew does not separate the two mornings, that from the roots is Mark’s own detail, and that Peter being reminded is owed to Peter’s telling — it almost sounds, he adds, as if Peter blamed Jesus for what he had done. Barnes heads that off: to curse here means to devote to destruction, and does not imply blame.

The dried root is then read as a nation. Pseudo-Jerome makes the day a figure: the Lord, leaving darkness in the hearts of the Jews, went out as the sun to another city well-disposed and obedient, for the sun sets in one place and rises in another, the light taken from the Scribes shining in the Apostles; the withered fig tree is the synagogue. Bede presses the roots to the same end: dried from them to show the nation was impious not only for a time and in part, and was to be smitten for ever, not merely afflicted from without and then freed; or else that it was stripped of the favour of heaven as well as of man, losing its life in heaven and its country on earth. Henry keeps it general: all wither who reject Christ, and we should rest in no religion that does not make us fruitful in good works.

The promise about the mountain embarrasses two. Bede reports the objection openly: the Gentiles who attack the Church say we have never had full faith, since we have never been able to change mountains. He answers that it could be done if necessity called for it, and cites a bishop of Pontus by whose prayers a mountain once yielded a city as much ground as it wanted; or else, the devil being often called a mountain for his pride, the removal is of him. Chrysostom bounds it differently: as the Lord did not dry the fig tree for its own sake but as a sign that Jerusalem should be destroyed, so the promise about the mountain is to be taken, though such a removal is not impossible with God. Clarke reduces the difficulty by grammar: have faith in God is a Hebraism for the faith of God, that is, the strongest faith, as the mountains of God means exceeding great mountains. Barnes reads it likewise, as confidence that God can do with ease what appears most difficult; Gill notes that the mountain is the Mount of Olives, near which they then were.

On the praying itself the notes turn practical. Ellicott reports the better reading, believe that ye received them, and takes the words of spiritual rather than temporal blessings: we are to believe not that we shall one day have what we ask, but that we receive it as we pray. Robertson calls that the test of faith, the kind that sees the fulfilment before it happens. Theophylact describes the experience: whoever sincerely believes lifts his heart to God and is joined to him, his burning heart feeling sure that he has received. Cyril of Jerusalem takes the asking to its highest object, that the heavenly Father gives the Holy Spirit to them that ask. On posture Barnes holds that God looks on the heart rather than the position, and that anxiety about a form should not exclude anxiety about the soul. Wesley asks who could find fault if the Creator destroyed by a word a thousand inanimate creatures, were it only to imprint this lesson more deeply on one immortal spirit.
27:
Who is asking, and why, is settled at once. Robertson notes that the three named groups were all in the Sanhedrin, so a large committee of it, Sadducees and Pharisees together, confront Jesus in a formal attack on his authority for cleansing the temple. Theophylact supplies the motive: angry at his casting the traders out, they came to tempt him — as if to say, who art thou, dost thou make thyself a doctor and ordain thyself Chief Priest? Henry adds the legal shape: they claimed a power to call prophets to account for their mission, and if they could show the people he had none, they would tell them they ought not to hear him — the last refuge, he says, of obstinate unbelief. He notes too that Christ walked in the temple not for diversion but teaching, as the Peripatetics were named from walking when they taught. Robertson dissents in one line: the question, in all three Gospels, was a perfectly legitimate one.

What the dilemma meant to catch is agreed. Theophylact sets the horns: if he said by mine own power they might seize him; if by another’s, they might make the people leave him. Bede goes further into the malice: by what authority doubts its being the power of God and wishes his work understood as the devil’s, while who gave thee this authority denies that he is the Son of God, since they grant the miracles but refer them elsewhere. He adds why the counter-question was prudent, not evasive: the Lord might have confuted them directly, but puts a question so they should be condemned either by their silence or their speaking. Robertson agrees it was no dodge but a home thrust, clearing the air and defining their attitude to John and Jesus alike, for they rejected John as they reject Jesus; the demand answer me he takes for Mark’s own. The reason for choosing John is Theophylact’s: the Lord asks about him not without a reason, because John had borne witness of him.

Their private reasoning is watched closely. Gill has them withdraw to consult; Robertson says they see the horns sharply, knowing what Jesus will reply — they wish to break his power with the multitude, but a false step will turn the laugh on them, and they see it. Bede puts their fear in an order that damns them: fearing to be stoned, they feared still more the confession of the truth. Clarke reports the textual trouble in the second horn, many copies reading we fear rather than they feared, one editor dropping the conditional to make it a question. He draws the moral that envy, malice and double dealing have always a difficult part to act, and are confounded by their own projects, while simplicity needs no mask. They told the lie, he concludes, and escaped for the present.

On the answer itself the notes are small and sharp. Ellicott observes that the intensifier in that he was a prophet indeed is one of Mark’s graphic touches, and corrects the reply: better, we do not know, the repeated tell in the English giving an unreal emphasis absent from the Greek, where the stress lies on the pronoun. Robertson calls it a self-imposed ignorance, a refusal to take a stand about the Baptist, and notes they feared John dead as much as Herod had, his martyrdom having deepened his power. Barnes sends the reader to the challenge put to Moses, and the prophets who reproached Israel for not knowing. Pseudo-Jerome puts the exchange in a sentence: they envied the Lamp and were in the dark, of whom it is written that God ordained a lamp for his anointed and will clothe his enemies with shame. Gill dates it the morrow after the cursing, and observes that Jesus was nothing intimidated by such a body of men; Wesley refers to the parallels.
